items.title: How LinkedIn, Netflix & DoorDash Run Agents, Evals & Inference in Production: QCon AI New York 2026
items.summary:
QCon AI New York has published its full program for December 15–16, 2026. Engineers from LinkedIn, Netflix, DoorDash, Figma, Pinterest, Honeycomb, Harvey, Google DeepMind and OpenAI describe AI systems they run in production. Talks cover agent permissions and guardrails, eval loops, inference cost, AI code review, and team adoption.

By Artenisa Chatziou

Facilitating the Spread of Knowledge and Innovation in Professional Software Development Unlock the full InfoQ experience by logging in! Stay updated with your favorite authors and topics, engage with content, and download exclusive resources. Lily Mara explains how to avoid high-risk software rewrites through incremental FFI refactoring. She shares how engineering teams can replace Python bottlenecks with Rust via PyO3, demonstrating how to achieve dramatic function-level speedups, seamless integration testing, and meaningful infrastructure cost savings without microservice overhead. Agentic AI architecture extends microservices and cloud-native architectures with AI agents that work with context, memory, and protocols such as MCP and A2A. The article covers bounded-context integration, task-dependent coordination strategies, new security risks, and observability needs. It expects gradual adoption alongside existing architectures, with platforms absorbing common components. Aditya Mulik explains how Walmart Global Tech deployed multi-agent LLM workflows across 4,700 stores for nightly batch inventory forecasting. He discusses tackling production hurdles - schema violations, cross-department data mismatches, and network drops - via MCP grounding and loop agents, while slashing cloud inference costs from $100k+ to $10k per month shifting from PTUs to pay-as-you-go. Vanessa Formicola shares how technical leaders can move beyond "wishful architecture" by practicing holistic socio-technical engineering. She discusses why engineering leaders must account for organizational maturity, reward structures, geopolitical climate, and team dynamics, framing the staff-plus role as designing the conditions for technology to thrive rather than just picking tools. Oli Lane and Julian Wreford share how Gearset replaced guesswork in distributed asynchronous queues with OpenTelemetry tracing. They explain why traditional metrics fall short, how to implement user-centric SLOs based on latency distributions, and share practical debugging tips to help senior developers, software architects, and engineering leaders improve system reliability and team culture. items.title: Phala Confidential AI Compromised
items.story_key: story|title:phala confidential ai compromised
items.content_excerpt: We are publishing preliminary findings from a security incident affecting Phala infrastructure. Two groups of users may need to take action: We contained the incident on November 8. The affected model service has been restored with additional protections and monitoring. The attacker made further attempts after our KMS root key rotation on November 6, and we have observed no successful unauthorized access since containment. Our investigation and comprehensive verification of the remediation remain in progress. We are limiting exploit-specific details until this work is complete. We will then publish a full root cause analysis (RCA). We are sorry this happened, and we appreciate the patience of everyone checking their systems and rotating credentials. On November 5, we detected unauthorized activity on one server. The attacker chained a legacy internet-facing service with management interfaces that relied on loopback access for trust and did not independently authenticate callers. This allowed the attacker to create unauthorized CVMs and obtain application credentials. We blocked the identified access paths that day. On November 6, we rotated the KMS root key used to derive application secrets. On November 8 UTC, a third-party security researcher provided evidence that request data sent to DeepSeek V4 Flash 0731 had been exposed. We traced this evidence to an inference deployment on a new GPU server. It was serving production traffic without our full production security hardening. The attacker used a similar access pattern to take control of the inference VM, making in-flight request data visible during processing. We took the deployment and its model offline. The attack sequences and associated infrastructure overlap. Our current assessment is that a single actor conducted both intrusions, and we are treating them as one incident. All times are UTC. This is a condensed operational timeline, not an exhaustive forensic log. In-flight request contents may have been exposed for requests sent to Phala's deployment of this model during the window above. Treat any credentials or other sensitive information in those requests as compromised. From July 1 through November 7, the researcher regularly included unique, per-request canary credentials in requests to Phala and monitored them for subsequent use. items.title: Encoder Disaggregation in vLLM: Scaling Multimodal Serving with EPD
items.summary: Recent advances in vLLM encoder disaggregation: metadata-only multimodal requests, dedicated encoder execution, remote embedding transfer, cross-encoder caching, and lower-overhead EPD routing.
items.story_key: model:vllm|title:encoder disaggregation in vllm scaling multimodal serving with epd
items.content_excerpt: Multimodal inference adds an encoding stage before language-model execution. Images, video frames, and audio must be processed into embeddings before the language model can use them. The demand on this stage varies with media size, modality, and request mix, and can change independently of prefill and decode demand. Encoder / Prefill / Decode (EPD) disaggregation separates these stages into independently deployed vLLM instances. Recent work in the vLLM community has expanded EPD across model execution, remote embedding transfer, shared caching, multimodal input handling, and request routing. DeepSeek's inference deployment Q&A describes an E/P/D architecture with a separately deployed vision encoder. vLLM has supported encoder disaggregation since our December 2025 architecture post , and continues to improve that support. vLLM main now also supports metadata-only EPD for DeepSeek V4.1 Flash. This post explains the engineering behind that progress, with a focus on five changes: The EPD tracker links the ongoing work. The core vLLM capabilities described below, including MiMo and XPU support, are included in vLLM v0.32.0. DeepSeek V4.1 Flash metadata-only support is available on main through #62802 . The vLLM Router and SMG integrations below use their respective main branches. EPD supports two deployment patterns: E+PD , with a separate encoder and a combined prefill/decode instance, and E/P/D , with all three stages deployed separately. Figure 1. E+PD separates encoding from language-model execution. E/P/D additionally separates prefill and decode. EC connectors deliver encoder embeddings; KV connectors transfer the state between prefill and decode. An image-heavy workload may need more encoder capacity without a corresponding increase in decode capacity. A workload with longer responses may require the opposite. Separating the stages allows operators to adjust their instance counts and execution settings independently, while moving encoder computation off the GPUs serving the language model. Transferring embeddings solves only part of the handoff. The consumer also needs enough information to reconstruct the multimodal input layout: placeholder lengths, image grids, feature lengths, and identifiers linking those positions to the transferred embeddings. A straightforward EPD implementation sends the original media to the encoder, transfers the resulting embeddings through an EC connector, and forwards the original request to P/PD. items.title: Cutting LLM Token Costs with Currents News API and TypeSafe Jev Pre-Filtering
items.story_key: story|title:cutting llm token costs with currents news api and typesafe jev pre filtering
items.content_excerpt: Screening news with TypeSafe Jev before LLM synthesis cut input tokens 16–18% at a 0.70 threshold; blind judges could not tell five of six cells from raw. Currents News API keyword search is built for recall. A query for a geopolitical development or a stock ticker returns every publication that mentions the search terms, including wire duplicates, boilerplate press releases, and generic sector watchlists. An agent that summarizes this output pays frontier input prices for every article, on-topic or not, on every scheduled run. The two tiers differ by roughly 50–70× in input-token price. Frontier synthesis input currently runs $2.00–3.00 per million tokens; TypeSafe Jev classification input is $0.042 per million tokens. The practical answer is to move the relevance decision upstream: screen each candidate title and snippet with Jev, and send only retained candidates to the synthesis model. We built this pipeline end-to-end and measured it on live data: 2,000 candidate articles across two real news pools, 60 briefings from three synthesis models, and a blind panel that scored filtered versus raw briefings without knowing which was which. At the default 0.70 relevance threshold, screening cut downstream input tokens by 16–18%; five of six blind-panel quality cells were statistically indistinguishable from raw, and the sixth showed a small negative delta. Stricter thresholds screened out 30–52% of candidates. At frontier pricing, this nets roughly $10–17 per 1,000 screened 200-article batches per synthesis model. One 200-article candidate batch costs a frontier model roughly 35,000–45,000 prompt tokens, and a full 1,000-article pool costs roughly 174,000–223,000 per pass. A scheduled daily pipeline pays that on every run. The cost is not only financial. Tangential commentary and syndication duplicates also consume the model's attention budget and slow generation, because time-to-first-token scales with context length. Three questions determine whether screening helps: how much of a real keyword-search pool is irrelevant, how many tokens removing it saves, and whether the briefing degrades when filtered. This article measures all three on live data. Follow along with a free key. Free covers 250 requests/day with a 30-day lookback. TypeSafe Jev is a classification API priced at $0.042 per million input tokens, evaluated here with typesafe-sdk 0.6.0 . items.title: Joint Quantization and Dynamic Partitioning for Context-Aware Edge Vision Transformers
items.summary: Deploying vision transformer models across connected and automated vehicles (CAVs) requires joint management of computation and Vehicle-to-Vehicle (V2V) communication. Static split-inference methods use fixed partition points and cannot adapt to time-varying link bandwidth, processing load, and concurrent multi-stream traffic. This paper proposes an edge orchestration framework that jointly selects model partition points, per-layer quantization bitwidths, and execution placement across heterogeneous vehicular compute nodes. The joint partitioning and mixed-precision allocation problem is formulated as a Mixed-Integer Linear Program (MILP) that minimizes compute and communication energy subject to end-to-end latency and task-quality constraints. The framework is evaluated on Jetson Orin Nano (8~GB), Jetson Orin NX (16~GB), and Jetson AGX Orin (32~GB) nodes using OPV2V-driven multi-stream workloads with $K \in \{2,4,6,8\}$. Across the evaluated configurations, the proposed formulation reduces V2V communication energy by $33.3$--$36.0\%$ relative to a Uniform INT8 split. At $K=8$, end-to-end task completion latency is reduced by $34.0\%$ on the Orin Nano and $33.1\%$ on the Orin NX relative to the same baseline, while limiting the reduction in 3D detection accuracy to $3.1$--$4.1$ percentage points in $\mathrm{mAP}_{50}$ relative to FP16 execution.

items.title: Can KV Cache Be Reused Across Model Updates? A DeepSeek-V4-Flash Case Study
items.summary: Reusing key--value (KV) caches across language model updates could avoid repeated computation of shared context, but changes in model weights raise a fundamental question about what these caches preserve. We investigate direct cache reuse across four model updates, with a detailed study of DeepSeek-V4-Flash to Flash-0731. Our central finding is that caches can retain useful task information without faithfully reproducing the updated model's behavior. Retrieval accuracy varies substantially across updates, ranging from near-native performance to large losses. With source caches already available, reuse achieves median time-to-first-token speedups of $2.10$--$5.08\times$ on three longer-prefix QA benchmarks. To characterize the behavioral differences behind these outcomes, we introduce Functional Cache Divergence, which compares next-token distributions under reused and native caches. Direct KV cache reuse better preserves native model behavior in natural-text continuation, whereas compatibility degrades with increasing prefix length in single-token retrieval tasks. Answer-margin analyses help explain how correct retrieval decisions survive substantial internal state changes. Yet even agreement on the first generated token does not ensure agreement in answer content or stopping behavior. These findings establish task utility and fidelity to native inference as distinct criteria for evaluating cross-version KV cache reuse.

items.title: When Should Agents Remember? Falsification-Gated Self-Evolution for LLM Agents
items.summary: LLM agents increasingly operate in long-horizon, verifier-rich environments, but current self-improvement mechanisms often write episode-derived lessons directly into memory, making local success an unreliable signal for reusable and safe knowledge. This paper addresses the core question of when an experience-derived behavioral update should be admitted into persistent agent state. We propose Falsification-Gated Self-Evolution (FGSE), a verifier-grounded framework that represents each candidate lesson as a structured hypothesis with an explicit precondition, behavior change, expected effect, and verifier. FGSE applies the hypothesis only in a temporary state, tests it on target-transfer, falsification, and archived-regression probes, and then commits, refines, or rejects it according to measured gain and risk. Across web, app, tool-use, and long-term memory benchmarks, FGSE achieves strong task performance, including 39.8 WebArena success rate, 78.8 AppWorld average completion, and 0.724/0.487 Pass$^1$ on $τ$-Retail/$τ$-Airline, while reducing falsification failures to 5.0%, regression damage to 1.3%, and harmful committed updates to 3.6%. These results suggest that testing memory updates as hypotheses supports more reliable long-term adaptation.

items.title: GitHub affordances as human-agent conveyances
items.story_key: story|title:github affordances as human agent conveyances
items.content_excerpt: Thinking about how GitHub PRs and issues are becoming the primary surface for collaboration between humans and agents. I've been noticing the growing use of GitHub, or rather core GitHub building blocks, as the natural choice for work management between humans and agents. Specifically issues and pull requests. One example close to me and my colleagues is how my friend and boss Tom Jung manages the identification, parcelling and specification of tasks for his agents to work on, as issues in the repo for our tutorial system . Another example is how that work is then managed in the form of pull requests (PRs), which I guess is a natural consequence of the first observation. Incidentally, this makes me think that this also changes the issue mechanism as a conveyance for work items rather than mere problem statements. A net positive, perhaps. Anyway, it's on the topic of PRs that I came across two blog posts from folks I have admired for a long time. In Hide your slop PR descriptions behind <details><summary> , Simon Willison uses HTML's details disclosure element to avoid the TL;DR reaction "I'm not reading all of that" to super-detailed agent-written descriptions which, while not incorrect, are too deep for the purposes of overview by a human. In “Doctor, it hurts when agents create unreviewable PRs.” “Don’t do that.” , Jon Udell describes the problem of agents raising PRs with thousands of lines that that are nigh on impossible to properly understand. He maintains (and I agree) that the PR should be a shared context between humans and agents, and - while some would say that using agents to review such monsters would be one solution to that 1 - smaller chunks of work are the answer. Both approaches allow the PR to remain the unit of work for tracking and review, and make room for the human to still be the active arbiter in the decision process. In traditional terms, the PR can stay primarily a letter, rather than a ledger. With many others, both Simon and Jon are exploring the paths ahead with existing tools and mechanisms, coming up with approaches that are pragmatic workarounds which eventually become norms. Something that the online community has been doing for decades.

items.title: BotPsy: On-Device Personal Assistant with a Sub-Billion-Parameter Agentic Language Model
items.story_key: story|title:botpsy on device personal assistant with a sub billion parameter agentic languag
items.content_excerpt: Frontier cloud LLMs carry high operational costs that can fluctuate unexpectedly, and relying on such third-party models introduces vulnerabilities, as providers can modify, deny, or deprecate access at any time. Furthermore, proprietary models offer limited customization for specific workflows, while posing risks to privacy, data control, and transparency. Besides, not every task demands frontier-level intelligence: small, specialized agents can be equally capable on specific tasks and significantly cheaper to run, since many routine or smaller workloads can be processed efficiently on-device. As intelligence per parameter continues to improve rapidly, we aim to stand at the forefront of this shift toward performant, privacy-focused, self-hosted models. Tether AI Research introduces BotPsy , a 0.8B-parameter model introduce BotPsy , a 0.8B-parameter model designed for function calling and agentic workflows, built on top of Qwen3.5-0.8B and suitable for on-device deployment. BotPsy is a "personal assistant" that uses tools to perform a variety of simple tasks for the user, in domains such as web search & research, travel & lifestyle, commerce & finance, business & customer operations, device & vehicle control, files & documents, calendar, and email & messaging. Due to its small parameter count, it is best suited to tasks of low to medium difficulty. BotPsy achieves state-of-the-art (SOTA) tool-use and agentic performance for its size, outperforming every model of up to 1.2B parameters that we tested (Figures 1 and 2). Designed for secure on-device workflows, it provides exceptional instruction-following reliability and efficiency while keeping user data private. As a small model, BotPsy still makes mistakes and is not intended for high-stakes use; please read the Intended Use and Limitations for more information. We will take appropriate actions in response to notice of copyright infringement. If you believe your work has been used or copied in a manner that infringes upon your intellectual property rights, please email data-apps@tether.io identifying and describing both the copyrighted work and alleged infringing content to file a notice of infringement. (“Tether AI Research”, “we”, “our”) will focus on expanding on-device agentic capabilities to seamlessly integrate with an even broader array of hardware and local services. items.title: Continual-ARC: Measuring Skill Acquisition over a Working Lifetime
items.summary: Agent harnesses have emerged as a promising mechanism for continual learning, alongside test-time parametric learning. However, the current benchmarks have several limitations: they generally focus on a single applied domain, serve each instance only once, and assume a single family of learner, so memory-based and weight-based systems are rarely compared on the same scale. We propose Continual-ARC, a lifelong stream built from the three ARC-AGI editions, whose tasks need no domain knowledge. The same tasks return after dormant gaps with fresh instances, while new tasks keep arriving. On each instance, the learner may pay for demonstrations, submit answers, or act inside the harness, with retries permitted on incorrect submissions, which are paid for. Each instance is scored based on the share of this feedback budget consumed. Since a learner may keep anything between instances, memory-based and weight-based systems are scored on the same scale. After the stream, the learner is frozen and tested on fresh instances of the tasks it met, which measures memorization, and on unseen tasks, which measures generalization. We run an agent harness with frozen weights, with and without persistence, on Qwen3.5-9B and GLM-5.3 Flash, comparing them with two prompting floors, a program-induction method and Qwen3.5-9B's weights trained to imitate GLM-5.3 Flash. Persistence in the harness generally does not improve memorization unless provided with explicit expert guidance. Most harness-based methods still learn less than a floor that simply caches each task's demonstrations, across all models we tested. No harness-based method gains on unseen tasks, whereas weight-based learning shows substantial gains. This opens the door to future weight-based continual learning that could teach models to drive harnesses in new domains.

On the first day of AIE Code Summit, OpenAI showed how developers can steer Codex by voice, hand off work to the cloud, and make use of dots. AI Engineer Code Summit kicked off today with a series of workshops, including from leading frontier labs OpenAI, Anthropic and Google DeepMind. I attended the OpenAI workshop, intriguingly titled “New Ways of Working with Codex” and hosted by two of its Developer Experience engineers, Dominik Kundel and Charlie Guo . The past year in coding agents has been one of constant product upgrades by all the frontier labs. But not all of these changes have gone smoothly. The shift to cloud , for example, is still confusing to many users of Codex, Claude and Antigravity. We’ve also seen new ways to work with agents. Personal agents like OpenAI’s dots and Anthropic’s Claude Duet can assist between sessions, while voice mode gives developers another way to steer coding tasks. OpenAI’s workshop addressed all three, and I also had some followup questions on these topics for Kundel, after the session. Guo began the workshop by listing a selection of things they’ve shipped in Codex since the AI Engineer World’s Fair in June 2026. “I had to cull this list in order to make it fit on the screen because there were too many things to put in here ,” he said. “I think the team has been shipping at an unbelievable rate.” Codex launched in May 2025 as “a cloud-based software engineering agent that can work on many tasks in parallel.” But Kundel admitted that “it took a while for models and harnesses to equalize into something where we can build a really engaging experience.” In other words, the cloud part of Codex has often been an awkward user experience. That began to change after DevDay in late-September, when a revamped version 2 of Codex Cloud was announced. Suddenly, cloud usage seemed more viable. items.title: Edith Harbaugh: Code Is Cheap. The Last Mile Isn't.

Automated software delivery is moving faster than the people who used to approve every release. LaunchDarkly co-founder and CEO Edith Harbaugh tells Guy Podjarny why rollback should be autonomous, why one-shot coding agents fail, and why the bottleneck has moved to the last mile.

– Running a company in the agentic coding era, and why teams should take dumb bets

What we cover: – How automated software delivery and autonomous rollback take humans out of the 2 a.m. incident – What makes a good feature flag, and when a homegrown system stops being enough – Why coding agents need an explicit definition of success before they write a line – Where release management fits in an AI software factory – Feature flags for AI agents: switching models and prompts at runtime – Running a c Transcript (sampled): keeping them uh aligned as they make many, many of these decisions is uh is is is hard because you know it takes the same amount of time to talk to their you know colleague and sort of you know describe what it is that they're they're uh they're building, and it's still a pain or like a product discomfort if uh if if they're misaligned. Like … part, which is describe what what success looks like, what failure looks like, uh, what are the guardrails that you want them to stay within? You know, like what are what are you know what are the lines, like what's disallowed, what's allowed. And so you need to do, you know, what we oftentimes avoid and just saying like we'll know it when we … of the software factory is this like tickets to PR, but then the sort of the breadth of it thinks about the SDLC as a whole. Like, how do you think about Future Flags as a whole, but also maybe like Launch Darkley's place, right, in in that flow? Yeah, so it's it's it's interesting the software factory metaphor has really taken off, I'd say, … enough to remember Windows 95, like it came as this immense 32 disc blob, where it's impossible to say, hey, is this feature better than this feature? You just couldn't know it. But now with the ability to break down uh changes into smaller and smaller bundles, you can actually have a really good gauge of is this working? But you also want to … getting another and sort of seeing what happens. Uh correct, or um monitoring for errors. Um so if you have, for example, a chatbot that suddenly is getting a lot of customer complaints, um, you can dial it back or switch Swiss models, or uh if it's suddenly burning a lot of tokens, uh you can switch between models on the fly. Yeah. Who

items.title: LangSmith BYOC is now available on AWS, Azure, and Google Cloud
items.summary: LangSmith BYOC now runs on AWS (GA), Azure and Google Cloud (Beta). Your traces, evals, and agent deployments stay in your cloud account while LangChain runs it.
items.story_key: story|title:langsmith byoc is now available on aws azure and google cloud
items.content_excerpt: LangSmith Bring Your Own Cloud (BYOC) now runs on AWS (GA), Azure (Beta), and Google Cloud (Beta). Your traces, evals, datasets, prompts, and agent deployments stay in your own cloud account, on the cloud you choose, and LangChain manages the data plane for you, from orchestration and scaling to platform updates. By splitting the control plane and data plane in two, BYOC provides greater flexibily to decide where agents run and where telemetry lives, without taking on the work of running LangSmith. LangChain runs the control plane , which holds auth, org and workspace config, billing metadata, hashed API keys, and static UI assets. You own the data plane , which holds everything sensitive, from traces, prompts, and datasets to experiments, agent deployments, and workspace secrets. An organization can hold several data planes, each in its specific account and region, and each data plane holds its workspaces. This lets you split data planes by region, environment, or business unit. For example, a platform team might run production and staging data planes in separate AWS accounts, while a business unit that standardized on Azure runs its own, separate BYOC deployment on Azure. Each team's traces land in the account that team owns. Until now, teams with strict compliance boundaries deployed and maintained self-hosted LangSmith. This kept their data inside their own boundary, but it took dedicated platform engineers to patch stateful services, configure databases, and run schema migrations. With BYOC, LangChain provisions and operates LangSmith inside your own virtual network. Consider a team running agent applications across several environments. With self-hosted, every update to the execution components meant coordinating downtime and managing custom Helm rollouts in each environment. With BYOC, the data in your data plane stays in your VPC while LangChain handles scaling, schema updates, and runtime dependencies. While self-hosting continues to be a reliable deployment option for customers who require complete control, BYOC provides the best of both worlds for customers who need it. Since we launched BYOC on AWS in August, many teams have chosen to run LangSmith in their own cloud with BYOC. They point to three main benefits: By expanding LangSmith BYOC to Azure and Google Cloud, more teams can get access to this experience while choosing their preferred cloud vendor. Each cloud has its own network policies, identity model, and security requirements, so BYOC

items.title: claude-code v2.1.321
items.summary:
What's changed

  • Added Claude Fable 5.2 (claude-fable-5-2), now the default Fable model — 1M context, $8/$40 per Mtok with $0.20/Mtok cache reads
  • Added --settings <file> to claude remote-control, which applies a settings file to every session it starts; if the file changes, no new session starts until you restart claude remote-control
  • Fixed MCP OAuth requests sending secrets such as refresh tokens to another host when a server redirected them
  • Fixed a case where a read-only Bash command ran outside the sandbox without a permission prompt
  • Fixed a case where Bash permission checks judged a file write from the wrong folder and didn't prompt
  • Fixed deny rules and protected-file prompts not applying to the file that a cp or mv into a directory writes
  • Fixed the "Draws from usage credits" note showing after a switch to Fable on Enterprise seats whose plan includes Fable
  • Fixed the fallback model sometimes declining a request or mentioning a stopped response when the first model was blocked before replying
  • Fixed claude mcp login printing a SEP-2352 issuer warning each time you sign in again to a server that Claude Code registered with
  • Fixed NotebookEdit deleting or overwriting a notebook's first cell when the call named no cell, on network paths (UNC shares, WSL folders, /net mounts)
  • Fixed Edit changing the first of several matches, replacing a whole file on an empty old_string, or editing a notebook as text, on network paths (UNC shares, WSL folders, /net mounts)
  • Fixed /config showing Manual as the default permission mode when new sessions start in auto mode; pressing Space on "Auto (default)" now saves Don't Ask, not Plan
  • Windows: Fixed FileChanged hooks stopping for paths set through watchPaths after the first shell command, when the session's working directory had a lowercase drive letter
  • Fixed --plugin-dir . and --plugin-dir ./builtin writing generated type files for Claude Code's built-in plugins into a builtin folder
  • Fixed context usage estimates overcounting tool definitions when exact token counts are unavailable
  • Fixed /compact showing twice in Remote Control on web and mobile
  • Fixed plugin auto-updates and /plugin marketplace updates downloading a plugin again for each worktree or folder of a repository
  • Fixed auto mode losing a background subagent's report that had started a turn when the conversation was compacted before Claude answered it
  • Fixed project skills, commands and agents staying missing after their folder was removed and came back mid-session, such as with git stash, including after entering a worktree
  • Fixed claude -p sometimes telling Claude that background commands get 30 minutes when they are stopped after 10
  • Fixed pkill, pgrep and pidwait in cloud sessions matching the session's own parent processes
  • Fixed Claude in Chrome and computer use server processes staying alive after their parent exits behind a proxy that stalls connections
  • Fixed a large hook output pointing Claude to a file that held another hook's output from the same tool call
  • Fixed apps that embed Claude Code getting their own PreToolUse hook's ask reason instead of another hook's when both asked
  • Fixed a PreToolUse hook's ask being lost when another hook's defer finished first and could not be honored
  • Fixed a rare crash on permission prompts and background tasks
  • Fixed project skills, commands and agents disappearing from the menu in SDK and desktop sessions after Claude entered a worktree
  • Fixed /desktop on macOS saying Claude Desktop is not installed when it is in ~/Applications
  • Fixed OpenTelemetry repository attributes (vcs.*) missing from Claude Desktop sessions that start on a pre-started process
  • Fixed WebFetch passing "No response from model" to Claude as page content when the model reading the page returned no text; the call now fails with a clear error
  • Fixed screen reader mode delaying the prompt at startup when the system clock moved back while Claude Code was starting
  • Fixed a command's panel sometimes not coming back after a dialog closed, leaving no panel or prompt on screen until the next redraw
  • Fixed a project's MCP server being disconnected after the first message in a Claude Desktop Code tab session when the desktop app has an MCP server or extension of the same name
  • Fixed a turn ending with "API Error: EPROTO: The TLS handshake failed" when the connection broke partway through a reply; the partial reply is kept or the request is retried, as before 2.1.302
  • Fixed high memory use in long sessions that repeatedly read single lines from large files
  • Fixed fast mode losing replies, switching models or retrying for minutes when fast serving is rate-limited, overloaded or failing; it now tries standard speed on the same model first
  • Fixed one request carrying far more background agent reports than intended after Claude was stopped while several were waiting
  • Fixed messages from a Claude Desktop Code tab session to your other sessions staying paused after you typed while Claude was still working
  • Fixed claude agents ignoring --permission-mode, --dangerously-skip-permissions, --model, --effort or --agent typed before agents when a flag such as --verbose was also on the line
  • Fixed a case where Remote Control showed as off with "login expired" in the desktop app while its connection was still up, because the app was briefly unable to hand over a sign-in token
  • Fixed a Remote Control message sent with "Queue for later" reaching Claude in the middle of the running turn
  • Fixed the git status given to Claude at session start reading as clean when git status failed; it now reads as unavailable
  • Fixed the git status given to Claude at session start showing the first listed file as staged when its changes were not staged
  • Fixed a hang or out-of-memory crash when a connector in a cloud session lists resources with very long names
  • Fixed Remote Control showing as connected after its connection closed for good while the session's history was still uploading
  • Fixed screen reader mode turning off when you return to a conversation from agent view
  • Fixed screen reader mode y/n questions taking as yes a stray "y" at the end of text typed as the question opened
  • Fixed cloud sessions telling Claude that a host is probably not allowed when it is allowed and the network proxy could not connect to it
  • Fixed an MCP server sometimes showing as connected with no tools after it was reconnected or the session's directory changed while its tools were still loading
  • Fixed Bash commands sometimes running in the wrong folder when Claude sent several at once and an earlier one changed folders
  • Fixed files Claude sends from cloud and Remote Control sessions failing at once when an upload gets an HTTP 507 from a proxy; the upload now gets a second try
  • Fixed new messages not being saved, and claude -p, SDK and VS Code sessions hanging, when memory ran out while the transcript was being read
  • Fixed sign-in, token refresh and logout waiting indefinitely when something on the network accepts the connection but never answers the TLS handshake
  • Fixed a sent file showing under a different name in the Claude apps when its name hid text-direction or control characters; Claude now refuses to send such a file
  • Fixed sub-agent progress summaries running a request to its end after the model replied with a tool call
  • Fixed Bash reads such as grep -r foo "$PWD/src" asking for permission when the same command with the path typed out runs without asking
  • Fixed Claude apps gateway refusing to start when a desktop setting holds a field newer than the gateway, such as a managed MCP server's oauth.omitResource; it now warns and serves it
  • Fixed Bash commands coming back empty for zsh users whose .zshrc sets KSH_OPTION_PRINT
  • macOS: Fixed "Unable to read managed policy settings" at startup when a valid MDM profile was slow to read: the read is retried once, and a timeout is now reported as a timeout
  • Fixed agent view erasing another agent view's saved input text when it restarted for an update with nothing typed
  • Fixed remote sessions giving no reply after a restart when a UserPromptSubmit hook blocked a replayed permission answer; these hooks no longer run on that replay
  • Fixed claude remote-control accepting a y typed without Enter at its first-run question when the terminal's input ended
  • Fixed Claude Desktop not showing spend limit warnings behind a Claude apps gateway whose policy has no code: rules
  • Fixed fullscreen sessions with some plugins ending with an error when a tool result that had got shorter scrolled off the top of the screen
  • Fixed prompt suggestions making extra API requests when the model replied with a tool call
  • Fixed PreToolUse mcp_tool hooks on stdio and HTTP MCP servers being skipped when their answer was over 16 MiB; the tool call is now refused
  • Fixed skill and command names holding a Bamum letter that some fonts draw as blank: they are now refused
  • Fixed claude -p on Linux exiting 0 in silence when a full NFS export or a used-up NFS quota lost transcript lines: it now prints an error and, in text and json output, exits 1
  • Fixed background agents being reported as stopped by the user, and refused a resume, when a service interrupted a cloud session and nobody pressed Stop
  • Fixed NotebookEdit reporting success to hooks and telemetry when the edit failed, for example when the notebook changed while the permission prompt was open
  • Fixed a blank screen or no answer at startup, and empty claude mcp list output, when a stored MCP sign-in record was null
  • Fixed the Artifact tool telling Claude to add filters when an artifact's database collection is too large to sort; it now says to read the collection page by page and sort the results
  • Fixed a restarted cloud session dropping a message with a large image when the restart came before Claude's first reply to it
  • Fixed a restarted cloud session leaving a subagent's message to the main conversation unanswered
  • Fixed Claude not being told when you stop or pause a running workflow, so it no longer says the workflow is still running
  • Improved the /model picker: "More models" is now an unnumbered row below every other, and older models open under it without renumbering the rest
  • Gateway: Improved spend limits on a busy replica, which now skips fewer checks and records spend sooner
  • Improved the Claude apps gateway's sign-in limit messages in Claude Code and on the /device page: they no longer name gateway settings, which the gateway's own log still names
  • Improved claude install and the install scripts: they finish 2 to 4 seconds sooner
  • Improved how soon a Remote Control session whose process crashed can pick up a new message
  • Windows: Improved startup and first-command time by finding programs on PATH without starting a helper process
  • Improved auto mode in headless sessions, the desktop app and VS Code: reports from background subagents that wait together are answered in one model call, as in the terminal
  • Improved the agent view's row for a claude --bg --worktree session that couldn't set up its worktree: it now shows the error from its beginning, not an internal tag or its last 200 characters
  • Improved the messages shown when an artifact is in another organization: /login is offered only if it's one of yours, and Claude now says where a copy may be after an account move
  • Improved sessions with more images than fit in one request: Claude is told whether it has already seen a dropped image, and repeat reads of an unchanged image are limited
  • Improved claude remote-control's messages for an unanswered first-run question: each now says what to do next
  • Improved start-up time by loading trusted TLS certificates faster
  • Improved Claude apps gateway error messages to show the gateway's address without any user name or password
  • Improved the Claude apps gateway's spend limit error: the reset now shows in your local time, such as "resets 4pm (America/Los_Angeles)"
  • Windows: Improved startup time with a standard Git for Windows install by no longer checking which git.exe to run on every launch
  • Updated the session-feedback message and the allowedProviders setting description to name Ultra alongside Pro and Max, and the forceLoginMethod description to cover every paid Claude plan
  • Updated the bundled dataviz skill to suggest a list of meters, one row per item, for several ratios that each have their own limit
  • Updated the "Upgrade to Max" options to say "Upgrade to Max or Ultra"
  • Changed mods Claude writes to turn on without asking in auto and bypass modes, even with managed allowUnsandboxedCommands: false or allowManagedDomainsOnly, and not to load in dontAsk mode
  • Changed mods' own tool calls ($.tool.call, $.mcp.call) to raise no permission prompt, even under your own ask rules or in dontAsk and -p runs; deny rules and organization policy still apply
  • Changed saved Fable 5.1 model picks to move to fable: on Pro and Max plans at once, on Team and Enterprise plans once your organization allows it; use /model claude-fable-5-1 to switch back
  • Changed the fast mode labels in /fast, /config and /model to name your current model when it supports fast mode, and removed "(Opus only)" from the VS Code row
  • Changed nested skill loading: .claude/skills folders inside ~/.claude/plugins no longer load when Claude works on files there
  • Self-hosted runner: Changed an on-demand runner that the server refuses because it is not needed (session ended or paused, work order superseded) to exit 0 instead of 1
  • Windows: Changed how Claude Code finds programs it starts itself, such as git, to skip relative and UNC PATH entries and links onto a network share, and to pick up PATH changes from settings
  • Changed OpenTelemetry hook events in non-interactive sessions to leave two built-in hooks out of num_hooks and num_success after Bash and PowerShell calls
  • Changed the number of messages a Claude Desktop Code tab session can send to your other sessions before it waits for you to type again from 10 to 20
  • Changed AskUserQuestion in claude -p and SDK sessions to deny a host's permission answer that sets the undocumented afkTimeoutMs input field
  • Changed managed extraKnownMarketplaces: a declared name can't be added from another source, an entry from elsewhere is hidden, and plugins the declared marketplace lists are reinstalled from it
  • Changed Claude in Chrome tools that an app running Claude Code provides, such as the Claude desktop app's Code tab, to follow your organization's Claude in Chrome policy
  • Changed policy_mode: layered in the Claude apps gateway: managed MCP servers now add up over every matching policy, match: {} included, so a gateway already on it serves more after the upgrade
  • Gateway: Changed Bedrock, Vertex and Foundry upstreams to ignore the ANTHROPIC_*_BASE_URL variables in the gateway's environment. Set base_url on the upstream to use another endpoint
  • Changed headless sessions to reload mods in .claude/skills when their files change; set CLAUDE_CODE_PLUGIN_DIR_WATCH=0 to turn this off
  • Changed the Cyber Verification Program sentence on a cyber safeguard block to use the same words as claude.ai
  • Changed Cowork cloud sessions: a PostToolUse hook can no longer replace the answer to AskUserQuestion or the plan in ExitPlanMode's result; Claude reads the originals
  • Changed cp and mv spelled by a path, such as /bin/cp, to get the same path checks as cp and mv
  • Changed background command notifications and TaskStop results to show Claude only the start and end of a command over 1,000 characters, which saves context
  • Changed artifact design guidance to treat Inter and Space Grotesk as good default typefaces
  • Changed the account email check to refuse only a shell command that holds your email and names a User-Agent, without asking, so other commands and scheduled runs no longer stop at its prompt
  • Changed Remote Control sessions to keep the folder they were started in: a connected client can no longer move a session to another folder
  • Changed managed extraKnownMarketplaces take-overs from an undeclared source: saved data is set aside for cleanupPeriodDays, and options and secrets until claude plugin restore-set-aside
  • [VSCode] Added a warning above the prompt box when both an auth token and an API key are set, matching the terminal's startup warning
  • [VSCode] Fixed a plugin's permission request showing a name with hidden characters: it now reads "a plugin"
